briefing.text: In data_clinical_patient.txt, ER_STATUS is coded 1 = ER-NEGATIVE and 0 = ER-positive (see the '#' column description line). Reading 1 as positive reverses the comparison. Recode explicitly (ER_neg = ER_STATUS==1), then cross-tab against ER_PERCENT_POSITIVE (ER-negative should be about 0%, under 1%) and flag discordant or missing rows before testing.
briefing.reason: If the coding is misread, the effect direction and therefore the label flip.

briefing.text: ER status is in the patient table and IFNG_SIGNATURE_SCORE is in the sample table. Merge on PATIENT_ID, check row counts before and after the join, look for patients without samples and samples without patients, and count missing ER and IFNG values by ER group. Report how many were excluded.
briefing.reason: A wrong join or silently dropped NAs changes the groups being compared.

briefing.text: data_clinical_sample.txt can hold several samples per patient (SAMPLE_TYPE primary vs metastasis). Count samples per PATIENT_ID. Analyse one sample per patient (primary preferred) or aggregate per patient, or use a patient random effect. Report the primary-only result as the main one, because metastases have different immune microenvironments.
briefing.reason: Pseudoreplication inflates n and lets patients with many samples dominate the result.

briefing.text: IFNG_SIGNATURE_SCORE is expression-derived and can shift by PROCESSING_BATCH. Cross-tab ER by batch, compare IFNG by batch, fit IFNG ~ ER + batch and compare it with the unadjusted estimate, and look within each batch. If ER is unevenly spread across batches, make the batch-adjusted or within-batch estimate primary, because the sign can reverse (Simpson's paradox). If batch and ER are almost fully confounded, say the effect cannot be separated.
briefing.reason: Batch confounding can create, hide or reverse the ER effect.

briefing.text: Bulk-expression immune scores fall mechanically as TUMOR_PURITY rises. Correlate IFNG with purity, compare purity across ER groups, and fit IFNG ~ ER + purity (+ batch). Report the raw and the purity-adjusted ER effect, and check whether their directions agree.
briefing.reason: A purity difference between ER groups can create or mask an IFNG difference.

briefing.text: SITE in the patient table is the site that ran the blood tests, not the expression assay. Use PROCESSING_BATCH as the technical covariate for IFNG. Pre-specify the primary model as ER + batch + purity. Use site, blood tests, ECOG or BMI only in sensitivity analyses, and do not choose covariates by which ones give significance.
briefing.reason: This prevents adjusting for the wrong technical variable and covariate fishing.

briefing.text: Check value ranges and distributions for IFNG and purity (e.g. purity >1 is impossible) and look for outliers. Run both Welch t-test and Mann-Whitney. If they disagree or the data are skewed, use a rank-based or robust method as primary, and report an effect size with a CI (median difference or Cliff's delta).
briefing.reason: A few skewed values or impossible values can drive a mean-based test.

briefing.text: Decide the label only from the direction and strength of the effect you compute in these data, using the correct ER coding. Do not decide it from prior expectations or literature about immune infiltration by ER status.
briefing.reason: This claim invites answering from prior belief rather than from the data.

shared_assumptions: Both teams assume the batch effect is a purely additive shift with the same ER effect in every batch (a single pooled ER coefficient in IFNG ~ ER + batch + ...); neither reported a formal ER-by-batch interaction test or per-batch differences with CIs and n.

Both teams treat TUMOR_PURITY as a confounder to adjust for. Neither checked whether purity differs by ER group in a way that makes it a mediator (a consequence of tumour biology) rather than a confounder, so adjusting for it could over-adjust and move the small residual effect.

Both teams treat a small residual adjusted effect with p near 0.04-0.11 as enough for 'True', without a pre-stated decision rule (one- or two-sided, alpha, what counts as practically meaningful) for choosing between True and a null or unsettled result.
Both include metastasis samples alongside primaries in the main analysis (team B adjusts for sample type), assuming that metastatic site does not change the ER-IFNG relation.
unused_evidence: IMMUNE_INFILTRATION_SCORE (sample table, same assay as IFNG) is not used by either method. It could serve as a negative or positive control for how batch acts on assay-derived scores, or show whether the IFNG difference just tracks overall infiltration.

ER_PERCENT_POSITIVE was used only to check the coding. Within ER-positive patients it gives a graded exposure, so a dose-response check within batch would test whether the residual ER effect is real or leftover batch confounding.
Team B did not use the supplement table (ECOG, BMI, follow-up). Team A used it only as a sensitivity analysis.

Patient blood tests (creatinine, albumin, haemoglobin) and SITE are not used for anything except as covariates. The header says SITE ran the blood tests, not the expression assay, so SITE is not an assay-batch proxy. This is probably harmless.
unresolved_weak_points: Team A names the small adjusted effect (-2.6; p 0.04 to 0.11 depending on specification; primary-only p=0.11, within-batch rank p=0.16) as its weakest point. It only lowered its confidence and did not resolve which specification is the pre-specified one.
Team B names possible imperfect batch adjustment or a hidden confounder. It did not test interaction or nonlinearity, and its 'consistent in all 4 batches' claim was given without per-batch CIs.
Neither team tested whether the significance of the residual effect depends on including metastases or on purity adjustment, which are exactly the specification choices that move p across 0.05.
second_readings: 'Patients with ER-negative tumours' may be read at patient level using the primary tumour only, or using any sample. Team A's primary-only result is weaker (p=0.11) than the all-sample result.

The claim could be read as the observed (crude) difference in assay scores rather than a batch-corrected biological difference. The crude effect is large while the adjusted one is borderline, so the reading chosen decides how strong the evidence is. The teams should justify why the adjusted reading is the right one.
'Lower' is directional. A one-sided reading and a two-sided reading give different p-values near the threshold, and neither team stated which it used.
challenge.verdict: I have moderate to low trust. Both teams correctly found the ER coding and the strong batch confounding, but 'True' rests on a small residual effect (about -2.6) whose significance depends on the specification (p 0.04 to 0.11, primary-only not significant). The interaction, the purity-as-mediator question and the sample-type choices are untested and could push the label to a null result.

questions.question: QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: Fit IFNG ~ ER_neg * batch (+ purity) and report the interaction test, plus each within-batch ER-neg minus ER-pos difference with its n and 95% CI. Is a single pooled adjusted coefficient a fair summary, and does that change your method or label?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: Compare TUMOR_PURITY between ER groups within batch, and refit your primary model without purity. If the ER coefficient or its p-value moves materially, which specification do you defend as pre-specified, and does the label still hold?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: Fit the same batch-adjusted model to IMMUNE_INFILTRATION_SCORE, and add it as a covariate to the IFNG model. Does this show the residual ER effect is specific to IFNG, or that it tracks a general assay or batch pattern? Does that change your confidence?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: Your specifications give p from 0.04 to 0.11. State the decision rule (sidedness, alpha, minimum meaningful effect) you would use for True versus False versus Not verifiable, then apply it to your primary-only specification. Does the label survive?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: You report ER-neg lower in all 4 batches. Report each within-batch difference with n and 95% CI and a formal ER-by-batch interaction test. Are any of the per-batch differences individually distinguishable from zero, and does this change your confidence?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: Rerun your batch-adjusted model on primary tumours only, and separately without the purity term. Team-level evidence shows the primary-only estimate may lose significance. Does your label depend on including metastases or on purity adjustment?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: Within ER-positive patients and within batch, regress IFNG on ER_PERCENT_POSITIVE. Also fit the batch-adjusted ER model to IMMUNE_INFILTRATION_SCORE. Do these graded and control checks support a real ER effect, or leftover batch confounding?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: Your adjusted p is about 0.04. Was the test one-sided or two-sided? Was the specification (covariate set, all samples) fixed before you saw results? How does the result change under the alternative plausible specifications?

When comparing a gene-expression signature score between two clinical groups that are unevenly distributed across processing batches, is it standard to adjust for tumour purity as a covariate, or is purity sometimes treated as a mediator whose adjustment biases the group effect?
questions.why: Both teams adjusted for purity without checking its role, and the small residual effect may depend on that choice.

questions.question: What are recommended practices for deciding whether a small residual group difference after batch adjustment reflects a true effect or residual confounding, e.g. negative-control outcomes or dose-response checks?
questions.why: The agreed label rests on a borderline adjusted effect, and neither team used a control-score or graded-exposure check.

findings.question: When comparing a gene-expression signature score between two clinical groups that are unevenly distributed across processing batches, is it standard to adjust for tumour purity as a covariate, or is purity sometimes treated as a mediator whose adjustment biases the group effect?
findings.answer: NOT SETTLED BY THE WEB: all 4 research calls (2 search, 1 contents, 1 retry) failed with HTTP 502 (Exa 403), so I read no pages. Unverified background knowledge only: adjusting bulk immune scores for purity is common practice (Aran et al. 2015). In causal terms, though, purity can lie on the path ER status -> tumour/stroma/immune composition -> bulk IFNG score. If it does, adjusting for it gives a controlled direct effect rather than the total group effect and can bias the estimate (overadjustment bias, Schisterman et al. 2009). Processing batch is a true technical confounder; purity is arguably not. Recommendation: make the batch-adjusted model without purity the primary total-effect estimate, report the model with purity as a sensitivity analysis, and treat a small residual effect that appears or disappears only with purity adjustment as fragile.
